Almost every student we interview says the same thing, which is that they became more independent, and I have learned to be very careful with that sentence. It is not that I do not believe them. It is that the word was in the brochure, it was in the parents evening, and it was in the first email they ever received about the programme. So by the time somebody says it to me two years later, I genuinely cannot tell you how much of it is memory and how much of it is the phrase they were handed. What shows up in our data and almost never in the interviews is something much smaller. They come back able to tolerate not understanding. They stop needing to understand every word before they act, and that is worth more than the independence, and nobody mentions it, because it does not feel like an achievement. It feels like giving up. And one more thing, about the stories. Almost everybody describes a turning point. One bus, one match, one argument in a kitchen. The data does not show that at all. The change happens gradually, across weeks, with nothing dramatic in the middle. That is not people lying to me. That is how a human being organises five months when they look back on them.

I lost the habit within about two months of getting home, and I want to be honest about how fast it went. Over there I spoke English every single day, not because I was disciplined but because there was no alternative, and I think that is the part people misunderstand. I did not need much self-discipline abroad. The situation decided for me. I got up at that hour because training was at that hour. I spoke English on the bus because the person next to me did not speak anything else. Back here, nobody decides for me, and that is exactly the moment self-discipline actually starts, and I was not ready for it. So the routine went, and I used to be annoyed about it, and now I just plan around it. What I never lost, and I have thought about why, is that I am not afraid to start a sentence I do not know how to finish. That one survived because it is not a habit. It was a decision I made once, on an away bus, and you do not have to make it again every morning.
